lesson_title: Paying Chemistry to Run Uphill: Electrolysis
hook_text: There is dirt on a refinery floor worth more than the metal above it. Electricity put it there.
clip_script: A battery is chemistry volunteering — the reaction wants to run, and you collect the energy. Electrolysis is chemistry conscripted: you pay at the wall socket to force a reaction uphill, and the payoff is everywhere in your house. Proof one: your phone right now. In use, its battery rolls downhill like any galvanic cell. On the charger, the socket drags the same reaction backwards and rebuilds the chemicals — one device, two identities, every single day. Proof two: the copper refinery. A dirty slab dissolves off the positive electrode while pure copper lands on the negative one, and the gold, silver and platinum trapped inside refuse to dissolve at the tuned voltage. They just let go and sink. That sludge is collected and sold — dirt so valuable it helps pay the refinery's electricity bill. Proof three: salt water. Concentrated brine plus current equals three industries: chlorine for safe drinking water and PVC pipes, hydrogen for fuel, caustic soda for every bar of soap you own. And the famous no-show: sodium ions queue at the electrode and get turned away, because an electrode is an auction, not a queue — water outbids them and hydrogen streams off instead. Forced chemistry, bought by the kilowatt — and it built half of modern life.
visual_style: A ball hauled up a slope by a motor wired to a wall socket; a corroded copper slab shedding glittering grains into tank-floor sludge; a brine tank branching into three product streams — a tap of clean water, a fuel flame, a bar of soap.
mood: Industrial payoff — the economics of forced reactions, delivered as three proofs.
pacing: Volunteer-versus-conscript setup, three proofs with a beat each, auction reveal, wide-angle close.
